utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Should we now have the witness in again. Would you call the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-42-T, the Prosecutor versus Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stringer. If I could remind you that your affirmation from yesterday still holds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, it's Mr. Rodic, I think, is going to cross-examine. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, good day. I am counsel for General Strugar, and I will put some questions to you about your testimony of yesterday. You said that you worked in the Ministry of Defence in London from 1962 to 1965 and that the last four years you were the director of security in the Ministry of Defence, in charge of physical security of persons, buildings, and facilities. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in the Ministry of Defence between 1962 and 1995, not 1965. Otherwise, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you became director of security of the security department.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this on your return from your mission to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, before this appointment, what did you do in the Ministry of Defence? What post did you hold and what duties did you perform?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the immediate period prior to my going to Dubrovnik, to Croatia, I was what we call an inspector of establishments, looking after the financial and manpower requirements of the Royal Air Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what schools you completed, how long you attended those schools, and when you graduated from them.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, first of all, attended St. Ignatius College in London until 1950. Between 1950 and 1953 I was at Mercers' School in London, which is run by the Mercers' company. I then went to the University of Southampton to study navigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you graduate from that university?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I graduated, but it is a non-degree graduation in that I went into the merchant navy as a navigating officer cadet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have any diplomatic experience or as a soldier were you ever sent on a mission abroad?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my national service, I was sent to Cyprus on active service. During my reserve service in the territorial army I also went to Aden for a short period on active service, and during my career with the Ministry of Defence, I also went to Washington, at the British embassy there as head of the British defence staff administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us precisely where and when you did your national service.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My national service was between 1957 and 1959, and the bulk of it was done in Cyprus after initial training in England.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this military training in the navy, because you mentioned the merchant navy. So could you clarify this, please.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I served in the merchant navy between 1953 and 1957 but had to retire from that due to poor eyesight. It was then, because I was under 25 years old at the time, that I had to do national service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you spent 13 years in the Territorial Defence and that you are a reserve major. Throughout these 13 years, were you constantly in the reserves or were you simply on a list of reserve officers?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was constantly on the reserve list with the territorial army throughout that period, but left in 1951 when I had to go to Northern Ireland as the command secretary for the army there. Not 1951, I beg your pardon, 1971 -- 1973. I beg your pardon. I must get my dates right. Thinking back, it was 1973 that I left the territorial army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you were leaving England to go to this mission in the former Yugoslavia, you said that you received a briefing in the intelligence service of the Ministry of Defence as well as a briefing by the ambassador of the mission in Zagreb. Can you tell us in greater detail what information you were given at those briefings and what you were told about the situation in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the precise details of those briefings at this time - it was rather a long time ago - but essentially it was, as I stated earlier, a general briefing on the situation pertaining in Yugoslavia at the time, that the Croatian and the Yugoslavian armies were in conflict at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did they explain what sort of conflict this was?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Between whom did this military conflict take place, where, and why?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict took place in Croatia between the Croatian forces and the Serbian army, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know why this conflict broke out? Did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the precise details of the situation at the time except that Croatia wanted independence from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time, and this resulted in what I suppose effectively you could call a civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you know more about the social organisation of Yugoslavia? You mention the Federation of Yugoslavia. Do you know how many republics there were, what peoples lived in those republics? Did you know anything about the history of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did read about the history of the former Yugoslavia before I went, from books, and I was briefed on the disposition of the ethnic groupings within the Yugoslavian Republic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I will try to summarise the questions I have put so far by asking you whether one could say that at the moment of your arrival in Yugoslavia, due to your briefings and what you had read, you were familiar with the political situation in the former Yugoslavia in 1990 and 1991. Would that be true or not?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be basically true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know, then, who the regular armed forces were in this period, according to the constitution of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your view, what would the Croatian armed formations be then?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On what basis do you put that, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He's asking him for an expert legal opinion as to how one would characterise the legality of the Croatian armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I didn't see in it a request for a legal opinion rather than a general appreciation, but maybe I didn't understand the question correctly. Perhaps, Mr. Rodic, can you tell me more fully what it is that you're seeking to get.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour. Precisely what you just mentioned. In view of the former questions, the previous questions about Mr. Stringer's education, military experience, and the briefings he was given before leaving for the former Yugoslavia, and his knowledge of the situation with which he was familiar, knowing that the JNA was the regular armed force according to the constitution of the former Yugoslavia, I'm asking him for his opinion as to how he viewed the situation and the Croatian armed forces in connection, of course, with this conflict. This is not an expert opinion but his personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Weiner, I propose to allow the question despite your objection, but I do so on the basis that the witness, A, is not a legal expert; B, is not giving an expert legal opinion but is giving a general factual impression in his answer. Have you lost the question by now, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have got the question, actually, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, all I can say, I think, at this point in time is that when we went there, there was a de facto situation with the JNA as the federal army, but also a Croatian force which was uniformed. Now, the legal definition as to whether the Croatian force was a legal entity I can't comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stringer, yesterday you also said that you had read something about Dubrovnik as a city, about its significance. So I would like you to explain more about what you knew and what you had read about Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd read, of course, that it was an ancient city of cultural importance, and it was defined as a World Heritage Site, of course a great tourist attraction, and of commercial significance to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you answered part of my question, so I'll repeat it: Before arriving in Yugoslavia in 1991, had you ever been there before, in Yugoslavia or in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And when you gleaned this knowledge about Dubrovnik, you mentioned that it was a World Heritage Site. Did you ever come across information that this city was demilitarised before being declared a World Heritage Site?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that a World Heritage Site cannot be occupied by armed forces, that it is in fact a demilitarised zone effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you are aware that in that period and before the war there were no military facilities in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the following, please: Do you remember when, on how many occasions, and where you talked to the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to them on two occasions, I believe, in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On those two occasions, can you tell us in what year that was and where?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last year, at the Ministry of Defence in London, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were both those interviews in 2002 in the ministry or was there something different?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were both held within the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And did both interviews take place in 2002?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my recollection goes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And during both interviews did you talk to the same investigator?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about the period of time that lapsed between the second and first interviews.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been at least six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why the interviews were held in the Ministry of Defence? Because, as we heard, you are retired and have been since 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: My understanding is that my duties in Croatia at the time, that I went there -- I went on behalf of the Ministry of Defence, so they did have an interest in this, but it was also to ensure security that these interviews took place within a secure Ministry of Defence building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please don't hold this against me, but don't you feel safe in England if you talk to an investigator outside the Ministry of Defence building? As a retired person, you were invited to an interview with an investigator, and as far as I understand, you shouldn't be in any danger.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was a question of being in danger. Indeed, I was asked if I would like to be interviewed at home, but it was more convenient for the investigator and for myself to have the interview in London, and being within the Ministry of Defence building was convenient if nothing else. And the security is not so much to do perhaps with physical security of the person but with any documents that there might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you contact, in connection with these talks with the interrogators, anyone from the Ministry of Defence? Did anyone talk to you about the importance of these interviews or that you had to talk to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody said that I had to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who did you talk to from the Ministry of Defence on this subject then?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to the officials who are responsible for the former Yugoslavian desk within the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were these officials from the intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you say more specifically, then, from what service were they?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were general civil servants like myself, administrative civil servants.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What specifically did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically that it would be helpful if I told the investigators what I knew and what I was aware of, but there was no obligation on me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that the investigators of the Tribunal got in touch with you through the Ministry of Defence and not personally?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a procedure for investigators to approach witnesses in the United Kingdom, and this is done, I believe, through the Foreign Office and the Ministry of Defence as a former Ministry of Defence employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And did you on that occasion talk with the representative of the ministry about the details of those interviews; i.e., the documents? Did you seek any documents from them?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, you indicated before that two interviews took place in the year 2002, and as far as you could recall, about six months had elapsed between the two interviews. Did you also draw up and sign with the investigators a statement on both occasions or what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only on the second occasion that I drew up a statement and signed it in the presence of the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And during the first interview, was any record made, any minutes taken? Did you sign anything during the first interview?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I handed over some papers that I had which I took with me because I thought they might be of use.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when it was that you handed over these papers that could be of some use? Was it during the first or the second interview?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This refers, if I understood you correctly, to all the documents.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have here a statement with data on the witness Stringer, Adrien Paul, and the date and the place, the venue of the interview given, is the 6th and 7th of March, 2001, and 26th and 27th of March, 2002. The interview was conducted in the Ministry of Defence of the United Kingdom in Whitehall, and this statement was signed on the 27th of March by you personally and on the part of the investigator. Is this the statement that was the result of your talk with the investigator?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I haven't seen the statement. It must be the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the usher kindly distribute this statement. Please also provide a copy of the statement to the witness for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honour, for clarification, are they using this to impeach the witness or are they introducing this as an exhibit, or what are they doing? Are they tendering this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment, all that's asked is for the statement to be identified. We haven't yet learnt where that's going. I'm waiting too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I confirm that this is the statement, yes. The answer, Mr. Rodic, was that that is the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course it is the intention of the Defence, with the aid of this statement, as well as to verify the credibility of the testimony of Mr. Stringer, meaning that this statement also refers to subjects and contents that were the subject of yesterday's examination-in-chief. And whether we shall also tender it into evidence is something is that we should decide after having completed our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it that you are to suggest that there are matters in this statement which differ from the evidence given yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. And I think that answers your question, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour, but is the policy here on impeachment by prior inconsistent statements that the full statement is tendered to the Court or is the statement only tendered to the Court if it is offered as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To that I don't know the answer, Mr. Weiner, let me say. At the moment, we have them in front of us, but we will see. It will assist us in following the cross-examination on the document to have it. Whether we keep them afterwards will depend whether or not it becomes an exhibit or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No problem. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. If you'd continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, as you have confirmed that this is indeed your statement that you gave to the investigators, in the statement, the time when you performed the -- conducted the different talks with the investigator is different. It is not a six-month lapse between the two interviews but, rather, over a year, and they were not both conducted, both interviews, in the year 2002 but one in 2001, and then after over a year the second interview was conducted when this statement was drawn up and signed. As this is the near past, can you tell us, please, why these differences occur?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply my faulty memory. The original interview was clearly in 2001, but over a period of two to three years it does become slightly difficult for me to recall precisely that time frame, which is why I said there was at least a six-month gap between the two interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we then note that the same goes for your memory for a period of ten to 11 years back?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When questioned orally about events that happened 12 years or so back, clearly one's memory is not entirely fresh, which is why I have to occasionally refer, to jog my memory, to my diary, which is an accurate, in my opinion, statement of the events as they happened at the time. The problem is, as I think you will understand, sir, that when questioned about individual conversations that took place, it's almost impossible to recall exact details from memory, which is why we have this statement here, which is a transcript, basically, of my notes taken contemporaneously whilst in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I fully understand you, Mr. Stringer, but what I really wanted to know is whether precisely the content of this statement and your memories are mainly based on your notes or the diary that you consulted when you gave your statement to the investigators in connection with the substance of your statement, namely that in that connection you used the diary and your notes rather than what you could remember.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand the question, yes, I used the diary and my notes rather than my memory for the substance of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would you remember all the names, all the events had you not used your notes?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not remember all the names had I not got my notes in front of me. The events certainly are fresh in my memory, but getting them in chronological order over a period of a week, you know, may be a little difficult without reference to the notes and the diary itself which is set out in chronological order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, as yesterday, you said that you refreshed your memories by consulting your notes which you have preserved, if I understood you well, and yesterday you said that you have kept all the copies of your diary and the documents sent to you and to others. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, where was it that you kept these documents?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kept them in a secure safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And why did you keep those documents at all, copies of these documents for a period of 11 years?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For historical interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you also keep other official documents in this way?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in connection with my defence work. This was quite separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But you said that precisely during your mission you were also an official of the Ministry of Defence, meaning that we can also view these documents through the Ministry of Defence just as those documents while you actually worked at the Ministry of Defence in London that you came by during your term of office. Did you copy those also and keep them in a safe?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these are not Ministry of Defence documents, these are documents of the European Community Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Then can we say that these are official, that this is official documentation of the European Community's Monitoring Mission in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it allowed for such official documentation to be copied and taken to one's home for private purposes?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to be done also with the official documentation of the Ministry of Defence in London that you handled?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's not classified documents, and these are not classified documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you said that since the time that you returned from your mission in the former Yugoslavia to the time you met with the investigators, you had all these documents, all these copies that we have been referring to yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Awhile ago to my question you replied that you handed over the copies of these documents which you kept in your safe to the investigator during your second interview when also you drew up and signed a statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought I said that I handed over copies of the documents to the investigator at the time of my first interview, and it was at the second interview that we signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You're right. I apologise. You said that you handed over all the documents to the investigator during the first interview. Can you tell us where the originals of these documents are?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware where they are at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you at all hand over the originals to the European Community's Monitoring Mission, or are you keeping them as things of historical value?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The originals were handed over and filed, as I understand it, by the mission itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the usher please -- Prosecution Exhibits P1 and P4, can she present them to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This document marked P2 is, if I'm not wrong, a letter addressed to you signed by a Lieutenant Colonel General Milan Ruzinovski. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are we dealing with P2 now or P1?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It says P2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You first mentioned P1, and then specifically mentioned P2, as I followed it, Mr. Rodic. You've got me lost as well as Mr. Weiner. Which document are you wishing?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. This is document P1, that is the letter addressed to Mr. Stringer, signed by a Lieutenant Colonel General Milan Ruzinovski. The B/C/S version and the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the document which is the English translation of the B/C/S version, is there a -- is there your signature at the bottom of that version?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My initials, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when it was exactly that you affixed your initials to this document?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 26th of March, 2002, according to the date on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is the date also written in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Will you please now look at document P4. This is a handwritten report dated 10th of October. Do you have that document? Is it your signature at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And who wrote the date on it?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 7th of March, 2001. I did. It's clear that my memory was faulty in regard to the handing over of the document P1 at the original interview. This was clearly handed over at the second, and it was simply a slip of mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you reply to my question why were not all the documents handed over at the same time?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I think the second document, Exhibit P1, was a document which I found later, and after discussion with the investigator, it was thought that this would be helpful for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is there -- is it possible that the investigator may have given you this document?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the usher please also give the witness document P2.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have the B/C/S version in front of you? It is also a letter addressed to you by General Ruzinovski.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whose handwriting is this in this note under the signature of General Ruzinovski?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is mine, and the same date as the other letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it the same handwriting as the one in document P4? Because they do not look alike, but I have to ask you.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the B/C/S version of this document, P2 that is, is it your signature on the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And is the date written in your hand?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th of October, 1991? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this your handwriting? This is what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let's go back. Note on the B/C/S document, ADRM 03 number 02191321, the note written under the signature of General Ruzinovski, that is not your handwriting; right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know who wrote this?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall who wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Will you look at the English version, please, and tell me, is this your signature --

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: -- under General Ruzinovski?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And you also wrote the date?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can I take it then that you also handed this document to the investigator after more than a year relative to the other, previous documents?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. These were documents that were referred to in my diary notes, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please, so let us go back once again to document P4. At the bottom of that page, next to your signature, something has been added. Near the signature and the date, something has been added in handwriting. Can you read it for us.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's my handwriting and it says "Compiled in Dubrovnik on dates shown." I was asked to put that statement on it with my signature at the time that I handed the document over to the investigator, to confirm that this document was in fact compiled and written in Dubrovnik on the date contemporaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this diary of yours is right now?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have any special reason why you cannot say that?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. I handed over my copy to the investigator, and I assumed that the monitoring mission would have retained its copy, but I can't say where it is now, whether they kept it for a period of 13 years. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, does this mean that you no longer have in your possession these notes and this diary?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And these documents?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you keep them only for the sake of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware there was going to be a Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because you previously explained that you kept these documents out of historical interest, and yet you handed over these documents to the investigators, not expecting them to be returned to you.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is more important for documents such as this to be handed over to a Tribunal rather than be held by a personal individual. So just in the interests of justice, so that we can have the facts set out in the best possible manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In connection with this diary, can we call it a compilation of notes which, during your mission in Dubrovnik, you kept, as did your colleagues Nolan and Zak from the mission?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report, if I could just explain, that the -- each individual mission team would report back and submit a report of its activities as soon as possible after completion of the individual mission. Clearly, from Dubrovnik, it was only possible to submit a report at the end of our tour, which was, what, one week. Therefore, this document was written up at the time, day by day, and submitted as a report - which it states at the top, "Report of Team Bravo" - to the mission upon our return.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What I would like to clarify here is whether these notes are your personal diary in which only you jotted down your personal observations or is it a diary, the contents of which were entered by you perhaps but which constitute actually a compilation of all the notes made by all your colleagues for any particular day?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This -- each date's entry was made at the end of the day. It was a compilation of the notes by each member of the team, but we were all together on each occasion. So I transcribed these notes onto this report at the end of each working day. It was a compilation of the notes, if you like, made on the spot by the team, although I tended, because I was English, to actually write the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So we can agree then that this is a compilation of notes which you transcribed at the end of the day, but this compilation consists of notes made by all three members of the mission. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct insofar that I was the one that actually wrote notes during the course of the mission. We discussed between ourselves that my transcription of the events of the day was in fact correct so that we all three agreed that these notes were in fact a true reflection of what had transpired during the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you specifically: During the six or seven-day mission in Dubrovnik, did Mr. Nolan and Mr. Zak write down anything of their observations, meetings, issues raised during their contacts? In other words, did they make any notes at all during their mission in Dubrovnik and then show them to you so that this report or diary that you are talking about could be compiled?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the very best of my recollection, they made no notes as such. This was oral discussion between us as to what had happened, because we were all together at all of the meetings. I mean, none of us acted individually and separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I'm correct, you mentioned yesterday in one part of your testimony that Mr. Nolan was in Cavtat for a while, separated from you, in connection with the situation concerning shots fired, and can you then assert that Mr. Nolan and Mr. Zak, during your mission, made no notes of their own as to what they found?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nolan, at that time, was separated from us for about ten minutes, I suppose, but of course I can't say whether they individually made notes which they didn't show me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether they made any notes that they did show you on the basis of which they discussed the daily report with you.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can recall no occasion where they had made any written notes as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I'm very surprised that the other two members of the mission didn't use their pens when working in the mission. Can you tell me whether they read the final version of the daily report compiled by you?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. This was a report which was agreed between the three of us before it was submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did anyone sign these reports to show that they stood by their contents?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, to be perfectly honest. I have a feeling that we all signed a note at the end of the day, but I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see from the notes exhibited by the Prosecutor pertaining to these daily reports which you compiled, as you say, not a single one of them has any signature apart from your initials which were placed there only 11 or -- ten or 11 years later.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it usual for official reports to be sent without signatures?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these circumstances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether there was anything to prevent you or your colleagues from the mission from signing those documents at that time?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. It may be that we had signed or initialed a covering note on the top, but I can't recall it. The essence of the report is as stated there. The covering note, if there was one, I'm not aware where it might have ended up, if there was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether, apart from you, anyone else from the mission in Dubrovnik compiled reports pertaining to this period?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the specific period when I was involved in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said that you spent a certain period of time in the tasking cell of the mission in Zagreb before going to Dubrovnik, and you said that you visited barracks in and around Zagreb. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also said that after the mission in Dubrovnik, you returned to Zagreb. Can you tell me exactly what you did in Zagreb then in this tasking cell?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that tasking cell, as I recall it at the time, we were primarily concerned with the events in Vukovar which happened on the day that I returned. So we were making the necessary reports to the Presidency in The Hague about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So on your return to Zagreb, you dealt more with Vukovar and another mission went to Dubrovnik instead of yours. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another mission went to Dubrovnik, and we handed over to that mission when in Dubrovnik on the day that we left, which was the 16th of October, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The handwritten letters that were marked for identification yesterday bearing the dates 19th, 20th of October, and none of these letters or messages is addressed personally to you. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where did you get these documents from then?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents I obtained from the mission in Zagreb when the team returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were these documents addressed to you personally or to the mission in Zagreb, just as you sent letters to Zagreb while you were in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These letters, I understand it, were addressed to the specific members of the teams, the team that went out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But why, then, did you take these documents for yourself?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this wrapped up, as far as I was concerned, my mission to Dubrovnik. It just tied the loose ends up at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you then select for yourself official documents in the mission in Zagreb which you would keep and take with you?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were relevant to my mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But you handed over your duties in Dubrovnik before these documents were created, if I'm not wrong, because on the 16th you already left Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the messages that we are talking about refer to the next mission which came to Dubrovnik after yours, that had nothing to do with your mission, and the letters are dated three or fours days after your departure. Why then did you take these letters? These are official documents.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are documents which related to the events in Dubrovnik which again were of significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us until when you stayed in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 25th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have any other documents as there are five days to go until the 25th of October?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because as far as I can recall, nothing further significant occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So up to the 25th of October, as far as you know, and you followed the work of the mission, there were no significant events in Dubrovnik which would attract your attention?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't involved at that stage with Dubrovnik, and that was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As far as I could understand you, on the 19th and 20th, you were not involved in Dubrovnik either and yet you took the documents. These were two specific documents that were given to me, and I had no other interest in Dubrovnik after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who gave you these documents?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know the reason why these documents were given to you of all people?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was a change in the tone of the negotiations between the team that succeeded us and with General Strugar and the JNA at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what this has to do with my question in connection with the documents.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an interest -- an interesting development that had happened at that specific time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. Are you trying to say that the situation in Dubrovnik deteriorated after your departure?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly relations between the team and the JNA had deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And who reported this to you and what did it have to do with you?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall who reported this to me at this stage. It had nothing specifically to do with me except that I had been there at a critical time prior to the advancement of the front line around Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since, as you say, the mission in Zagreb also monitored the developments in Osijek, Vukovar, Zagreb as well as Dubrovnik and probably a number of other places throughout Croatia; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On your return from Dubrovnik, you said you dealt with the situation in Vukovar. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one of a number of people who were involved in the events subsequent to the evacuation of certain people from -- from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have in your possession the same sort of documents connected with Vukovar or Osijek or other places?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were the situations there not as interesting as the one in Dubrovnik as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not so personally involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will move on. Yesterday, you said that on the 5th of September, you arrived in Zagreb. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the investigators in 2001 and 2002, it says that you arrived in Zagreb on the 29th of September. It's on the first page, third paragraph on page 1 of your statement. So there is a discrepancy of almost a month.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 29th of September. I'm sorry, I can't identify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It's in the third paragraph from the top. The paragraph begins with the words, "In September 1991, I was requested by the Ministry of Defence to go to Croatia ..."

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see that. I think that must be a misprint.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you read the statement before signing it?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At the end, as far as I can see, you confirm that everything in the statement is true.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but occasionally there may well be a small error that one has overlooked in such a long statement, and for that I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. When you mentioned the mobile mission in Zagreb, yesterday you said that for the first seven days of your stay in Zagreb you visited barracks in and around Zagreb and visited the JNA troops that were in the barracks blockaded by Croatian forces, that you made sure that they had food and water, and that you monitored the situation to see whether the JNA would try to break out. My question to you, as you spent a long time in the army, is: Is this not an odd situation, and what did you think of it at that time, and what did you think of your role in that mission?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the whole situation was odd at the time, and the mission was there to try and calm things down and enable the two sides to reach amicable settlement of their problems. The JNA were confined within their barracks, and of course that was a peculiar thing to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that it's odd that a regular armed force of a country should be confined to barracks and that, with all due respect, as a foreigner in a mission you should visit them and monitor the situation to see whether they had enough food and water?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This question is: Do you agree that it's odd that a regular armed force of a country should be confined to the barracks. His opinion as to oddities is not relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I'm of the mind that I would allow the question. It's a -- there is some substance in what you put, but I think it very much reflects the general tenor of the cross-examination and what is being explored. We can understand that. Carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, my opinion is that it was a very odd situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you afraid that the JNA might try to break out of the barracks by force, you as a member of a mission with the task that you had?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I would also like to hear your opinion, bearing in mind your experience and the position you held, whether in view of the fact that this was a regular armed force which was in fact occupied by the Croatian armed forces and confined, whether that kind of break-out would have been legal.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on the legality of this situation, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: To put it more simply, in your view, is it a normal situation for a soldier to sit in the barracks and to be prevented from communicating or going out of the barracks? How would you as a soldier respond in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say how I would respond to such a situation because you can't be specific about this. All I can say is that it was a peculiar situation at the time, and we have to recognise the de facto situation, that they were confined in their barracks and surrounded by Croatian troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can such a situation become a source of conflict or tension in the area?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And did such situations happen throughout Croatia, as far as you know? Did you receive similar reports from other mission centres outside Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So could an armed conflict erupt because of such a situation?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your statement which you gave to the investigators, you said that on the 1st of October, 1991, the JNA launched an offensive against the municipality of Dubrovnik. You also said - this is the fourth paragraph of your statement - that "There had been no obvious political or military reason to launch such a campaign."

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was our opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you think that the events in Dubrovnik can be viewed in isolation from the overall situation in Croatia which we have just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, there were no JNA barracks being confined by Croatian forces in the area, and Dubrovnik was a demilitarised zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What period are you referring to when you say that Dubrovnik was a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring -- sorry. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say that Dubrovnik was a demilitarised zone, what period of time exactly are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, some of these statements - and I just want some clarification here - he's not -- he's attempting, I think, to impeach with prior inconsistent statements, but this is not inconsistent with his testimony. Some of this information we have not raised. He's asking these questions directly out of his statement, and these are not inconsistent with his statement. If he's going to do that, I think he should try to move and have the document admitted as a piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems to me that the whole document may be far wider than the purpose of this cross-examination. He's merely dealing with one particular issue at the moment. One of the effects of what is occurring may be that it will become admissible at your hands, Mr. Weiner. I don't feel there is reason to disturb what's happening at the moment. Carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. But perhaps to clarify this for our colleague, I said at the beginning why I was using this statement, and I said absolutely it was on account of the discrepancies between the content of the statement and yesterday's examination-in-chief. Of course, I can say right now that at the end of the cross-examination, we will indeed be asking for this statement to be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do I take it then, Mr. Rodic, that you'll be identifying some further matters that you say are discrepancies as you move through the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour, because it is of the essence for the Defence of General Strugar. And I should like to ask you another question, because we are not au courant with the actual schedule of this sitting. Is it the time for a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have been watching the clock and it's just a little past the time. I was waiting for a convenient time in your questioning, and by the sound of it, we've reached a convenient time, Mr. Rodic. But before we break, could we just be clear then so that Mr. Weiner is more at ease with the matter, that it is your intention to be tendering -- or seeking to tender this document at the conclusion of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I rather gathered that, Mr. Weiner. We will have, then, a quarter of an hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: From the contacts that you had during your mission in Dubrovnik with the representatives of the Yugoslav People's Army, did you obtain any information from them as to why they were there in that area around Dubrovnik and generally in the area and what the specific task of the army, that is, and the role of the army was in that area and the entire area of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were advised when we met with General Ruzinovski and representatives of his command that they believed the Croatians had taken up positions within Dubrovnik and were attacking their forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you believe such claims on their part?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our observations, we saw no such forces within the Dubrovnik city.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that at the time of your mission you did not at all see Croatian forces in and around Dubrovnik? I'm talking about Croatian armed forces.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only time I saw any Croatian armed forces was when we had a captain of what I believe was -- I think he was in the reserve forces of the Croatian army, and he came as a liaison officer for the Croatian army to one of our meetings with the JNA liaison officer, Captain Sofronije. And I believe there may have been some Croatian army personnel lightly armed with rifles at the time we left the port of Dubrovnik on the Slavija ferry after we had been returned there having been stopped in the Adriatic by a JNA warship. Otherwise, I saw no Croatian army forces at all, only civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. In your statement, also on page 1, paragraph 4 from the top you say: "To the best of my knowledge in this region there were no hostilities nor was there a major ethnic Serb population to protect, as the JNA and the Serbian government were claiming to be the case in other parts of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know at all, did you have any information as to whether there were any hostilities in the area that I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information by the time we got to Dubrovnik that there had been some hostilities in that part of the villages around the Dubrovnik airport had been shelled and also shells had fallen into the village of Cavtat and that there had been shooting around the -- Dubrovnik itself from the hills surrounding the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the preparations for war which were undertaken in Dubrovnik during the years 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the tasks which were assigned to the police and military units of the Croatians according to the orders of their commanders at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any cases of barriers being erected on communication links and roads? Do you know of cases of numerous attacks on military facilities, of military columns of soldiers in the area in the period 1990 by Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In 1991. I was referring to 1991.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware -- we believed that there were renegade Croat forces that may have attacked JNA forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify, explain what these renegade Croat forces were.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our understanding that these were not regular, if I can put "regular" in quotes, Croatian forces in the same way that there were also irregular Serbian forces which were allegedly attacking villages in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this statement that you made about the protection of Serbs, namely that there were no Serbs in the area, was not the story about the protection of Serbs just a cliche which you yourself also accepted and took for granted during your initial days of your stay in Zagreb and as you explained the situation in Zagreb as well as in other places in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I actually understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When in your statement you said that there was not an obvious political or military reason for launching a campaign around Dubrovnik, you said: "As far as I know, to the best of my knowledge, there were no hostilities in the area nor was there a major ethnic Serbian population to be protected, as the JNA and the Serbian government claimed to be the case in other parts of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. We could not understand why there should be any attacks on Dubrovnik itself. The fact that there may have been incidents that had occurred well outside the area was not, we thought, of itself reasons for any attacks to be made on Dubrovnik or areas where there were no apparent Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did it seem to you that there were no Croatian forces or do you assert that there were no Croatian forces in the areas in question?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot assert that there were no Croatian forces in the Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 393 to 398. area. We saw none.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was it a sufficient reason for hostilities if irregular Croatian forces were attacking the regular armed force of the former Yugoslavia at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, there was no sufficient reason for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of your statement, and this is the B/C/S version, you say that there are numerous assumptions why the JNA had attacked Dubrovnik. That is the last paragraph in the English version, on the first page the English version.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are hypotheses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I will read hypothesis number one, which is extensive, and it says: "The JNA recognised the tourist and economic potential of the region and the role it could play in the new Yugoslavia. The only way to achieve this was to intimidate the local population into leaving. The subsequent role and actions of the JNA appeared to be consistent with that of an organised campaign intended to expel the Croats from the region." Is this your assumption; and if it is, what is it based on?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not an assumption, it's a hypothesis, a number of hypotheses. We can't say which one is correct. These were views taken at the time, a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say -- when you say these were views taken at the time, are you referring to your personal view or I presume the view of the entire mission that you worked with?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is a general view of the mission, that this was one of the possibilities for the attack on Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I would also like to ask you in connection with the other possibility which you stated, which is that they wanted to use it as a bargaining chip for the release of JNA barracks from the Croatian bureaucrats in Croatia. Were you personally satisfied of the truthfulness of such a hypothesis? When I say this, I'm specifically referring to the fact that the barracks were blockaded in Croatia and so on.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't be truthful about a hypothesis. This is merely one of the considerations that one had to take into account as to whether it was a possibility that this is a reason for the attack. I'm not saying it was the reason, I'm simply saying that it's a possibility that it was a reason; and there were a number of these possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you participated in the mission, that you went out in the field, that you had extensive information on the basis of which you replied to my questions inter alia also on the blockade of the barracks, that is why I'm asking you. According to your knowledge and experiences from the area, could this second hypothesis be taken into serious consideration?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these hypotheses can be taken into serious consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you personally: Does your experience confirm the second or the -- the first or the second hypothesis more?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object to that. We're into -- we're into speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, I'm not sure whether you fully understand the significance of the word "hypothesis" in the paper -- in the statement of Mr. Stringer. He, I believe from his statement and his evidence, he is merely saying, "These were possible views that we took into account which could have justified the attack when, in our appreciation, we could not ourselves see that there was any military justification for the attack," and therefore, they searched around for possible justifications, and these were identified. I don't understand Mr. Stringer to be saying, "I firmly held this view or that view." He's merely saying these were the possible views that were held by the mission which could have justified the attack. So he's not really in a position to answer your last question, I don't believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that the shelling was indiscriminate and reckless at best. During your stay in the Dubrovnik area, was there any shelling, how much, and where?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the course of my stay there, we heard mortar fire in the background on the hills and Plat which is the hills surrounding Dubrovnik itself, and also rifle fire. And as you know, we did experience heavy machine-gun fire ourselves on our last day in Cavtat, which came from the JNA forces. But we had observed, of course, the destruction of houses in the area of Cavtat and in Cavtat itself, civilian houses, in areas where we could determine no indication of any Croatian or other military presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you personally see any houses that had been damaged in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly where? If you entered Cavtat, can you describe what houses in Cavtat were damaged?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We visited one house in Cavtat where the bedroom of a little girl had been damaged, and there was part of a rocket launcher - I can't say what kind - still lodged in the walls of that particular building. We didn't go inside any other houses, but we did see damage to houses, particularly on the route towards the -- towards the rendezvous where we met up with the JNA liaison officers, and also damaged boats within the area -- within the harbour of Cavtat. This had all been done just before or before we arrived. So we did not ourselves actually witness the shelling itself apart from the machine-gun fire we experienced on our last day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The damaged houses that you say you saw on the road leading to the place where the meetings were held, I believe that this is the road leading to the airport, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That's why I can assert that no houses were damaged in Cavtat nor was Cavtat shelled during that campaign. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I do have to say that the house that we saw and visited was in Cavtat itself and not one of the houses on the route out of Cavtat. The house we saw was where a little girl's bedroom had in fact been hit by a rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell me whether you saw any shelling anywhere during your stay in the area.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw no evidence of shelling other than what we heard in the distance. No evidence of current shelling, should I say, whilst we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What you heard as weapons in the distance being fired could have been directed at the other side, by one side -- any side against the other side. By this I mean not directed at the Dubrovnik area because there were operations taking place elsewhere. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now ask you to look at the following part of your statement where you say: "This is not to say that the Croats in the form of their defence did not provoke or breach the many cease-fires at the time." That is the fourth paragraph on page 3.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As you are evidently familiar with the many breaches of the cease-fires by the Croatian side also, can you tell us whether you saw these breaches, when, where, and how many approximately there were during the time of your mission. How many reports of this did you receive?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports of this during my mission in Dubrovnik, there were two reports, I believe, from the JNA side as to attacks against their forces where JNA soldiers had been killed. I'm not aware of further cease-fire breaches other than those that I stated in my statement. I would also -- I would, of course, regard the machine-gunning at Cavtat as a breach of the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did someone fire shots at you, the members of the mission?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shots went over our head sufficiently close to make us take cover. We did not believe that the attack was against us. We considered that in fact what was being shot at was a church on the side of the harbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did the Croats ever shoot at you?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: With the aim of frightening you or keeping you there?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one occasion which is when we left -- we were going to leave Cavtat where we were threatened by a Croat if we were to leave them alone, but my Polish friend who spoke a little language was able to calm him down and tell him that, you know, we were going and that was it. But otherwise, there were no occasions where we were frightened by or intimidated by Croatians, or indeed I must, in fairness, say the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, these Croats who tried to keep you there, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were trying to persuade us to stay and they were civilians, and they were really scared that if we went, they would be attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What weapons were these civilians carrying?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't carrying any weapons at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that these Croatian civilians fired shots at you in front of the Croatia Hotel in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to show the witness and to distribute to the other parties this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you first tell me whether you are familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a note I made. I think it was probably on my return to England.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this note refers to precisely.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to the incident where a patrol had moved forward on our last day in the area, had moved forward into Cavtat and where a loudspeaker announcement had been made to the villagers of Obod to return to their homes, otherwise Cavtat would be flattened, and where rifle fire or heavy machine-gun fire was directed from the JNA side across to what we believed was the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned this event yesterday, but I'm interested in something else now. I would like to know whether the signature on this document, on the first page, and there are initials on pages 2, 3, and 4, whether these are your signatures.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the date on the document, was it entered by you?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that you handed in this document to the investigators in 2001?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why this is the only typewritten document while all the others are in handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this, to the best of my recollection, was done upon my return to England.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I really cannot understand now why you would type this out in England if on the 16th of October you went to Zagreb where you stayed until the 25th. Wouldn't it be logical for you to compile the report while you were working for the mission and not to type it out in London?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly when this was typed. It could have been typed at the mission, or it could have been typed upon my return to England. It was simply an elaboration of my manuscript notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this the only purpose behind this typewritten document?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you do the same with the other documents that we discussed previously?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this was what we regarded as a major incident and we thought this was the beginning of the eventual attack on Dubrovnik itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you give this document to anyone?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you read out what it says under item 10 in this document.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
